title: Gitweaver
summary: A Git repository companion focused on making repository activity easier to explore.
problem: Repository work can become difficult to follow when branch activity, commit history and collaboration context are spread across different views.
approach: Gitweaver brings repository information into one focused interface. The project explores a server-backed workflow for connecting a GitHub identity and presenting repository activity in a more approachable way.
architecture: Express handles application routes and server-side requests.
GitHub OAuth provides the account-connection flow.
The interface presents repository, branch and commit information.
decisions: Keep the application centered on repository workflows rather than trying to recreate all of GitHub.
Separate server-side integration concerns from the browser interface.
Use a focused feature set that can be extended as the product grows.
learning: This project strengthened my understanding of OAuth-based integrations and the importance of designing around a clear developer workflow.

title: WA-Store
summary: A small-commerce storefront concept that connects product discovery with WhatsApp conversations.
problem: Small sellers need a straightforward way to present products online while keeping customer conversations close to the channels they already use.
approach: WA-Store combines a product catalogue and shopping flow with WhatsApp as a familiar communication channel between seller and customer.
architecture: Express provides the application routes and server-side request handling.
MongoDB stores product and application data.
EJS renders server-side views for the storefront.
WhatsApp links connect product interest to a seller conversation.
decisions: Keep the buying journey simple for small vendors.
Use a familiar messaging channel instead of assuming every seller needs a complex checkout stack.
Keep product and presentation concerns separate.
learning: The project helped me think about practical commerce workflows and how backend choices should fit the business model rather than add unnecessary complexity.

title: Insight-Ink
summary: A blogging platform exploring authenticated publishing and dynamic content management.
problem: A publishing platform needs more than a page that displays articles: it needs a way to manage content and associate actions with authenticated users.
approach: Insight-Ink explores a full-stack publishing workflow with user authentication and dynamic content management.
architecture: Express coordinates application routes and server-side logic.
MongoDB stores application and content records.
EJS supports server-rendered page views.
Authentication gates user-specific publishing actions.
decisions: Treat content management as a first-class workflow.
Keep persistence on the server rather than relying on browser-only state.
Use server-rendered views for a straightforward application structure.
learning: Building this project gave me practical experience connecting authentication, persistence and content workflows in one application.

title: AsoPay
summary: An invoice-management prototype designed around the day-to-day workflow of tailors and small businesses.
problem: Independent tailors need a simple way to prepare invoices, share payment details and keep track of whether a customer has paid.
approach: AsoPay focuses on invoice creation and customer-facing invoice views, with a demo payment flow used to explore the payment experience.
architecture: Seller-facing screens support invoice creation and management.
A shareable invoice view gives customers the payment context.
Payment states are reflected in the interface for the prototype flow.
A live payment integration must be separately configured and verified before real-money use.
decisions: Design the seller and customer journeys as connected but distinct experiences.
Make payment status visible instead of treating invoice creation as the end of the workflow.
Keep demo payment behavior clearly separated from production payment processing.
learning: This prototype pushed me to think beyond screens and consider state transitions, customer handoff and the trust required in payment-related products.

title: CodeWithFaith Chess Engine
summary: An independently implemented, CPU-first chess engine, built around correctness, search, evaluation and a portable UCI interface.
problem: A chess engine must do more than compile: it needs reliable legal-move handling, repeatable testing, efficient search and a way to connect to chess interfaces.
approach: CWF Engine is being developed as a layered engine with separate crates for chess rules, search, evaluation, UCI communication and executable orchestration.
architecture: cwf-core handles board state, FEN, legal move generation and game-history rules.
cwf-search implements iterative-deepening alpha-beta/PVS search and move ordering.
cwf-eval provides classical position evaluation.
cwf-uci exposes the supported Universal Chess Interface protocol subset.
decisions: Prioritize correctness and perft validation before optimization.
Keep rules, search, evaluation and protocol responsibilities separated.
Avoid unsupported playing-strength claims; use repeatable benchmarks and match testing.
learning: This project is deepening my understanding of systems programming, search algorithms, testing strategy and the engineering discipline required to build a complete engine.

title: CWF Store
summary: A personal app-store platform for showcasing and distributing applications built under the CodeWithFaith brand.
problem: Projects need a dedicated destination where visitors can discover app details, preview releases and access available downloads.
approach: CWF Store combines an application catalogue with app detail pages, download tracking, user feedback and an administration workflow.
architecture: Express provides the application API and server routes.
MongoDB stores app catalogue and user-generated records.
The frontend presents app discovery, details and account workflows.
Download endpoints support tracked distribution of uploaded application packages.
decisions: Treat app metadata and downloadable releases as separate concerns.
Provide administration tools for managing catalogue entries.
Keep download analytics and user feedback connected to individual apps.
learning: The project explores how a developer portfolio can grow into a product-distribution platform with catalogue management and operational features.

title: Co-op Lend
summary: A cooperative lending platform concept for member savings, loan workflows, repayments and ledger-based financial records.
problem: Many cooperative societies still depend on manual records, making savings, loan repayments and financial reporting harder to track and audit.
approach: Co-op Lend explores a digital workflow for member management, savings, loan approvals, repayment tracking and financial reporting, with Nomba integration planned for transfer operations.
architecture: Node.js and Express provide authentication, API and business logic.
MongoDB stores member, account, loan, ledger and audit records.
The loan workflow models repayment schedules and outstanding balances.
Nomba API and webhook integration support payment and disbursement workflows.
decisions: Represent financial activity through traceable ledger entries.
Design for duplicate webhook protection and reconciliation.
Separate the prototype workflow from any claim of live financial operations.
learning: This project has helped me think about financial state, transaction integrity, auditability and the backend responsibilities involved in payment-related systems.

title: CodeGuardian
summary: A JavaScript code-review helper that flags common code-quality issues and style problems.
problem: Small code-quality issues can make a codebase harder to maintain when they are not noticed during development.
approach: CodeGuardian provides a simple interface for submitting JavaScript code and receiving automated warnings for selected patterns and style checks.
architecture: Express serves the application and analysis workflow.
EJS renders the browser interface.
The analyzer checks for selected patterns such as var usage, empty functions and production logging.
decisions: Keep the checks understandable and actionable.
Focus the first version on a small set of recognizable JavaScript issues.
Present the results through a straightforward browser workflow.
learning: The project introduced me to building developer-facing utilities and translating code inspection rules into a usable interface.
